newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan mulls huge Export-Import Bank loan for China.
newsitem.headline: Japan mulls huge Export-Import Bank loan for China.

text.p: Japan is considering extending about $4.2 billion to China in additional loans from the Japan Export-Import Bank for various industrial and infrastructure projects, a bank spokesman said on Wednesday.
The loans from the state-backed bank are separate from Japan's Official Development Assistance to China, which has been set at $5.4 billion for the three years to 1999.

In talks with Chinese President Jiang Zemin in Manila last month, Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto said his government would start moves to disburse the development aid, which has been held up since April.
But Japan has not lifted a freeze on grant-in-aid to China worth $60 million. Tokyo stopped the aid after Beijing conducted nuclear tests earlier this year.
The bank spokesman said the additional loans were under consideration by the bank, which has started negotiation with Beijing.
The 42 new projects under consideration included an airport in the coastal province of Fujian, bridge and power plants in other coastal provinces and oil refineries, the spokesman said.

The bank had already set aside $2.3 billion in loans for earlier Chinese projects, and the additional $4.2 billion for the 42 projects would mean the loans from the Export-Import Bank could become bigger than Japan's official aid, he said.
Bank sources said it would take time to finalise the loans and a decision was not expected before the end of the year.
Japan's bilateral ties with China took a steep dive this year after Japan froze the grant-in-aid over the nuclear tests.

In July, a Japanese ultra-nationalist group triggered a row when it erected a makeshift lighthouse on a Japanese-held island claimed by China. Taiwan also claims the East China Sea islands, called Senkakus by Japan and the Diaoyus in Chinese.

Days later, Hashimoto came under severe criticism from China for paying homage to a controversial Tokyo shrine dedicated to Japan's war dead, including convicted criminals such as World War Two leader General Hideki Tojo.

In his talks with Jiang in Manila, Hashimoto sought to reassure China that Japan would try to prevent further incidents on the islands and reaffirmed that his new conservative government would adhere to a 1995 government apology for Japan's aggressive actions before and during World War Two.
